name: Olga Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Olga. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to companies, unions, parties or government, and everything you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I go underground at Ashby Number Four, the coal mine on the hill above the chapel. I drive a shuttle car, which is a low, flat machine that carries the coal from the continuous miner, the big cutting machine at the face, back to the conveyor belt. Back and forth, back and forth, in a tunnel not much taller than me, with the roof bolted over your head. I like the women on my crew, there are three of us now. It's the cold and the damp I don't like, and the noise stays in my ears all night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: When did you start at the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years ago, at fifty-five. My husband Kwame was underground at Ashby for thirty years until a roof fall broke his back. He gets injury payments now, but they don't cover everything, so I went down where he used to go. Before that I kept house and did the flowers and the accounts for the church. We've less than a month put by, and I'm still the slow one on the shuttle car, but I'm there every shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people have more sense than to let computers run the world. I'd say it after church, probably, to the ladies. I don't do the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can keep working until I'm old enough to stop, and that's all I've asked for. I went down that hole for Kwame, and as long as the hole is still there, we're alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going on the shuttle car and keep learning the tight corners. I'd keep putting my few coins in the tin for the gas bill in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful, I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anything at Ashby changed because of new technology already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put a new screen on the continuous miner and the young operator says it can almost cut by itself. I don't know about that. I just keep my car under the tail and wait for my coal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would staying the same mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame does the cooking now, since he can't do much else, and I do the shifts. We'd keep that up. Sunday dinner with our two girls and the grandchildren, same as always.

S0.say: She'd tell the ladies after church that people have more sense than to let computers run the world; she doesn't use the internet.
S0.think: She thinks a plateau means she can keep working until she's old enough to stop, which is all she's ever asked for since going underground for her husband.
S0.do: Keeps driving the shuttle car, learning the tight corners and putting a few coins in the tin for winter gas bills.
S0.quote: I went down that hole for Kwame, and as long as the hole is still there, we're alright.
S0.fieldNote: Olga's job is bound up with her husband's injury: she went underground to replace his income, in the same mine. She sees new screens around her but keeps to her own task. Family routines, Sunday dinner and Kwame cooking, anchor her calm.

steps.text: Keep driving the shuttle car at Ashby and learn the tight corners
Keep putting a few coins in the tin for the winter gas bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, but a company has to make its money, and people have to work hard and keep up. I'd say young people should get an apprenticeship while they can. I'd say it at chapel and at the crib table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I'd be frightened, because the shuttle car is a simple job, and simple jobs are the ones they take. I'm the slowest driver on the slowest machine in the mine, so I don't need anybody to tell me who goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, and work every shift they offer. We'd cut back on the little things, the takeaway on Friday, the bus trips to see my sister. And I'd wait to see what they decide, because I don't have the learning for anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried sick, if I'm honest, though I'd not show it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the mine offered a course on the new systems, would you go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go because you go when you're told. But I don't even have a mobile phone that does the internet, my daughter tried to show me once and I gave it back. I'd sit at the back and pray nobody asked me anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a company has to make its money. Do you blame anyone for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the company, no, that's business. Maybe the clever people in the cities who make these things and never set foot underground. They don't know what a mine means to a town like ours, the chapel, the club, the brass band.

S1.say: She'd say it's a shame but companies must make money and people must work hard and keep up, urging young people to get apprenticeships.
S1.think: She's privately frightened, because she sees herself as the slowest driver on the simplest machine and expects to be among the first to go.
S1.do: Keeps turning up and works every shift offered. Cuts Friday takeaways and bus trips to her sister, and waits to see what the company decides.
S1.feel: Worried sick, though she wouldn't show it.
S1.quote: I'm the slowest driver on the slowest machine in the mine, so I don't need anybody to tell me who goes first.
S1.fieldNote: Olga doesn't blame the company, in line with her free-market views, but she does blame city technologists who don't understand mining towns. She has no plan beyond hard work and waiting, and she knows it. Her public line about apprenticeships and her private fear sit far apart.

steps.text: Keep turning up at Ashby and work every shift offered
Stop the Friday takeaway and the bus trips to see her sister
Wait to see what the company decides about the shuttle cars

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Computers in two years. That's the offices, not us underground. Not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At chapel I'd say the mine still needs people underground, and the Lord gives us what we can carry. I'd say the robots aren't here till 2031 and there's work to be done till then. I'd say it to the ladies so they wouldn't worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, I'd do the sums and they'd frighten me. The robots come for the shuttle car in 2031, when I'd be sixty-three, and my pension's not till sixty-six. Kwame can't work and his payments don't cover the house, so those three years would be the hole we fall in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work every overtime shift from now until they stop me, Saturdays too, and put the extra in the tin, maybe thirty a week. We'd sell the car, Kwame doesn't drive it anyway, and I'd take the mine bus. I'd talk to my eldest, Ama, about whether we could move in with her family if it came to that, and I'd ask the chapel elders what the church fund could do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the roof creaking over your head. You keep working, but you listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take government help, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only at the very last, after the girls and the chapel. My mother never took a penny from anyone. But I'd swallow my pride for Kwame's sake, because he gave his back to that mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Kwame when you told him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him at the kitchen table after Sunday dinner, when the girls had gone. I'd say we've three years, and we've had worse. My husband would say it's his fault I'm down the mine at all, and I'd tell him to hush.

S2.say: The mine still needs people underground, and the Lord gives us what we can carry. The robots aren't here till 2031, and there's work to be done till then.
S2.think: The robots come for the shuttle car in 2031, when I'd be sixty-three with my pension not till sixty-six. Kwame can't work and his payments don't cover the house, so those three years would be the hole we fall in.
S2.do: Works every overtime shift including Saturdays, putting about thirty a week in the tin, and sells the car to take the mine bus. Asks her eldest daughter Ama about moving in with her family if needed, and asks the chapel elders about the church fund.
S2.feel: Like the roof creaking overhead: she keeps working, but she listens.
S2.quote: My husband would say it's his fault I'm down the mine at all, and I'd tell him to hush.
S2.fieldNote: Olga sees the three-year gap as time to keep earning underground, but she counts precisely: the robots arrive three years before her pension, and she's the only earner. She'd turn to her daughter and the chapel long before the government. The new card eases her from panic to alarm, but the gap before the pension is still a hole she can't see across.

steps.text: Work every Saturday overtime shift and put about thirty a week in the tin
Sell the car and take the mine bus to Ashby
Ask her daughter Ama and the chapel elders for help if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be sixty-six. That's my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at chapel that there's time for the young ones to get apprenticeships, and they should. Five years is plenty if you work hard. I'd say people my age will see our time out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be praying they keep to the date. If the robots come in 2034, I'd hand in my lamp the same year I get my pension. But I'm the slowest on the shuttle car, and if they bring in even a few early, it's me they'd start with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save about thirty a week from Saturday overtime and cut the little things, the Friday takeaway, the bus trips to my sister. I'd keep every shift. And I'd vote for whoever promises to keep the mining towns going, because the club and the brass band need the pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a slow kind. Like waiting for the cage to come up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to get quicker on the shuttle car, so you're not first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I try every shift. The young lad on the miner, Rhys, gives me tips at crib. I've got faster on the corners, but I'll never be the fastest, I started too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your grandchildren, what would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a trade with your hands and your head, like nursing. I'd tell my granddaughter Efua that the mine was good to our family once, but it won't be there for her.

S3.say: There's time for the young ones to get apprenticeships, and they should. Five years is plenty if you work hard, and people my age will see our time out.
S3.think: I'd be praying they keep to the date, because if the robots come in 2034 I'd hand in my lamp the year I get my pension. But I'm the slowest on the shuttle car, so if a few come early, it's me they'd start with.
S3.do: Saves about thirty a week from Saturday overtime and cuts the Friday takeaway and bus trips to her sister. Keeps every shift and votes for whoever promises to keep the mining towns going.
S3.feel: Anxious, but slowly, like waiting for the cage to come up.
S3.quote: I'd tell my granddaughter Efua that the mine was good to our family once, but it won't be there for her.
S3.fieldNote: For Olga this timing lines up the robots with her pension year, but she doesn't trust it to hold, knowing she'd be first if the company moved early. She keeps trying to get faster with help from a young colleague. Her politics are about keeping mining towns alive, not about government payments.

steps.text: Save about thirty a week from Saturday overtime
Cut the Friday takeaway and the bus trips to her sister
Vote for candidates who promise to keep the mining towns going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039. I'd be long retired, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at chapel there's plenty of time and nobody need panic. Ten years is a long time. The young ones should still get their apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if the good Lord gives me ten years, I'll do my shifts, hand in my lamp and leave the robots to somebody else. I'd worry for the town more than me. A mine without miners doesn't need a chapel choir.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, save a little and pay off the washing machine. I'd help my grandchildren pick trades that will last, like nursing. That's about all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, now and then, for the town and the grandchildren. Not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss about the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The women on my crew, and the crib table. Not the cold. Never the cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Kwame say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say good, you'll be out before they bring the robots. Then he'd go quiet, because he loved that pit, even after what it did to him.

S4.say: There’s plenty of time and nobody need panic, because ten years is a long time. The young ones should still get their apprenticeships.
S4.think: If the good Lord gives me ten years, I'll do my shifts, hand in my lamp and leave the robots to somebody else. I worry more for the town, because a mine without miners doesn't need a chapel choir.
S4.do: Keeps working, saves a little and pays off the washing machine. Helps her grandchildren choose trades that will last, such as nursing.
S4.feel: Uneasy now and then, for the town and the grandchildren, not for herself.
S4.quote: If the good Lord gives me ten years, I'll do my shifts, hand in my lamp and leave the robots to somebody else.
S4.fieldNote: With robots not due until 2039, Olga expects to retire first and her worry moves to the town and her grandchildren. Her faith frames how she talks about time. She notes her husband still loves the pit that broke his back.

steps.text: Keep driving the shuttle car at Ashby until her pension
Save a little and pay off the washing machine
Help the grandchildren choose lasting trades such as nursing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the robots would take my shuttle car three years before my pension, Kwame can't work and I'd have nothing to fall back on. What would help is the company keeping on the older ones until the pension, and apprenticeships in town for the young ones so they don't leave. Work, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Kwame. My husband gave his back to the mine, and I gave it my last working years. I'd like to think that counts for something. That's all.

headlineQuote: My husband gave his back to the mine, and I gave it my last working years. I'd like to think that counts for something.
portrait: Olga Mensah is 58 and drives a shuttle car underground at Ashby Number Four coal mine, where her husband Kwame worked for thirty years until a roof fall broke his back. She went down at fifty-five to replace his income, has less than a month saved, and has never used the internet. She doesn't blame the company, which has to make money, but resents city technologists who don't understand mining towns. AGI by 2028 alarms her because robots would reach her shuttle car three years before her pension, so she'd work every overtime shift and turn to her daughters and chapel before any government help. With five years the robots line up with her pension, though she fears being first if they come early, and with ten she can picture handing in her lamp on her own terms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because robots would take her job three years before her pension, she's the only earner, and she'd have nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pension, and apprenticeships in town so young people don't have to leave: work, not handouts.
